title: Steps to Kilometres and Miles: Why 10,000 Steps Is Not a Distance
h1: Steps to km and miles — the stride-length range and why trackers disagree
description: Average stride: 0.76 m (men), 0.67 m (women). 10,000 steps is 6.4 km for a 1.60 m person, 8.4 km for a 1.90 m person — same count, 30% distance gap.

hero: The famous '10,000 steps' goal is a step count, not a distance. Actual distance depends on stride length, which scales with height. A 1.60 m person walking 10,000 steps covers ~6.4 km; a 1.90 m person covers ~8.4 km. Fitness trackers estimate distance from step count and height — the estimate is 15–25% off in typical use.
body: The 10,000-step target came from a 1965 Japanese marketing campaign for the Manpo-kei ('10,000-step meter') pedometer, not from health research. Modern evidence (Lee et al. 2019, Paluch et al. 2022) suggests significant mortality benefit plateaus around 7,500 steps/day for adults and 6,000 for over-60s. Distance covered by those steps varies enormously by body size.
## The exact stride relationships

> Adult walking stride: ~0.415 × height (m)
> Adult running stride: ~0.66 × height (m) at 5:00/km pace
> Mean walking stride, men: 0.76 m (30 in)
> Mean walking stride, women: 0.67 m (26 in)
> 1 mile = 1609.344 m; 1 km = 1000 m
## Distance for 10,000 steps by height
The spread across a normal adult height range is ±15% around the median — enough that '10,000 steps' means very different workloads for two people walking together.
## Where the height × 0.415 rule comes from

Empirical study of adult walking gait finds stride length correlates ~0.83 with standing height, coefficient ~0.415 at self-selected walking pace. The relationship breaks at extreme paces: shuffling (0.35 × height), race walking (0.55 × height), and running (0.65+ × height). Fitness trackers typically use a single walking coefficient and are wrong for running.
## Cadence — the other half

Distance = stride × cadence × time. Typical walking cadence is 100–120 steps/min. At 110 spm and 0.75 m stride, that is 82.5 m/min = 4.95 km/h — the classic 'walking pace'. Doubling cadence (running) increases speed roughly linearly; increasing stride adds more per unit effort but requires fitness.
## Worked example — calibrating your tracker

Method: walk a known 400 m athletics track lane 1 (400.0 m) at your normal pace, count steps. If you take 520 steps, your walking stride is 400 / 520 = 0.77 m. Enter that in your tracker's settings; distance estimates now match GPS.
**Common mistake:** using the tracker's default (usually 0.762 m men, 0.660 m women). Tall women and short men get 5–10% error until they enter a measured stride.
## Fitness tracker accuracy in the field
Bassett et al. (2017) tested 10 wrist-worn trackers over measured walking courses:
- Best (Fitbit Charge 2): ±5% step count, ±8% distance.
- Median: ±12% step count, ±15% distance.
- Worst: ±25% distance.

Wrist-worn is worse than hip-worn (Manpo-kei style) because arm-swing amplitude is noisier than hip vertical displacement. Phone-in-pocket step counts (accelerometer) are typically ±10% of hip pedometer.
## Running is a different regime

Running stride grows with speed. At 6:00/km pace, adult stride is ~1.2 m at cadence ~170 spm. At 4:00/km, stride ~1.6 m at ~185 spm. Applying a walking stride (0.75 m) to a running step count over-counts distance by 60%. Trackers with a separate 'run' mode use GPS if available and fall back to stride estimates otherwise.
## Elevation matters

10,000 flat steps ≈ 300 kcal. 10,000 steps with 100 m elevation gain (typical urban commute up a hill) ≈ 380 kcal. Trackers that ignore elevation systematically underestimate hill workouts by 15–25%. Modern watches with barometric altimeters correct for this; phone-only tracking does not.
## The five-second recap

Stride length ≈ 0.415 × your height in metres. Multiply by steps for distance. 10,000 steps is 6–8 km depending on height. Calibrate your tracker with a 400 m track walk once — the default stride is wrong for most people.

faqs.a: At a moderate 110 steps/min walking pace, 91 minutes. At a brisk 130 spm, 77 minutes. Split across the day, most active people accumulate 5,000–8,000 without a dedicated walk.

faqs.q: Does step count include running steps?
faqs.a: Yes on wrist and hip trackers — any impact counted. Running cadence (170–190 spm) accumulates step count 50–75% faster than walking.

faqs.q: Are treadmill steps the same as outdoor?
faqs.a: Roughly. Treadmill stride is 5–10% shorter than overground at the same speed (missing air resistance, minor propulsive cheat). Trackers over-estimate treadmill distance by ~5%.

faqs.q: Why does my Apple Watch and iPhone disagree?
faqs.a: iPhone counts steps only when it detects the phone is being carried (accelerometer signature). The Watch counts arm movement. Disagreement is normal; combining both often double-counts.

faqs.q: What is a good stride length to aim for?
faqs.a: Do not force it. Natural stride is 0.4–0.45 × height. Over-striding causes braking forces at heel strike and injury risk. Improve cadence (aim 110+ spm walking) rather than stride.
